Setting custom colors

R uses a default color palate for colors
It is not ideal
You can override default colors with

scale_color_manual(): You define the colors
scale_color_brewer(): Use color scales from RColorBrewer
scale_color_viridis_<b|c|d>(): Use color scales from viridis

Brewer palates
The RColorBrewer is optimized for maps and has a variety of palates set using palette="<palate>"

Sequential (e.g., YlOrRd, PuRd)
Qualitative (e.g., Set3, Dark2)
Diverging (e.g., Spectral, PuOr)

A gallery is available in the R Graph Gallery

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Viridis Palettes
Viridis palates are designed

To be clear even if the viewer has common forms of colorblindness
To be clear when converted to greyscale
To have strongly contrasting colors with a logical order of progression

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Viridis Scales
The correct Viridis scale to use depends on your data:

scale_color_viridis_b()

Binned: Discrete with a defined order/ranking
Adjacent values have similar colors

scale_color_viridis_c()

Continuous: A range where any value is possible

scale_color_viridis_d()

Discrete: Discrete but unordered
Maximizes contrast between colors


What type of data do we have here?

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Viridis Colors
Viridis has several color range options

Set using option="<name>"
Possible names include magma, inferno, viridis, rocket, etc.

See all the options in the Viridis Documentation

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Other Important Viridis Options
The Viridis scale functions also have some other important options:

direction=[-1|1]

Sets the order of the colors. -1 reverses them

na.value="<color>"

Sets the color used when a value is NA
Set to NA for transparent

text:
Adjusting Legend Attributes
Many attributes of the way a legend is displayed are controlled by the plot theme

Change individual settings of the theme with theme()
Theme takes a series of named argument-value pairs
Named arguments define attributes of the theme
More complicated options controlled by guides()

See Tidyverse ggplot2 3.5.0: Legends for many examples

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Changing the legend position
The legend placement is controlled by theme attribute legend.position=

Possible values "left", "right", "bottom", "top"
"none" turns off the legend
"inside" requires legend.position.inside=c(x,y)

Places the legend inside at the specified x and y coordinates


Move the legend to the bottom of your visualization.

How does it change?

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Group-level calculations

Recall that you can place mathematical expressions in aesthetics
R will evauluate them and use the result to define the data displayed
You can use summary functions like mean()
By default R will compute the summary over the full dataset
Add the group= aesthetic to perform the calculation over each group

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Group-level Calculations
There may be occasions where you would like to perform a calculation specific to each group and visualize that result

A few options

Use mutate() combined with if_else() or case_when()
Use group_by() and summary functions
Use group= along with calculations in an aesthetic


Let’s think about implementing the group= method

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Example of a Group-Level Calculation
What will the following code do?

ggplot(data=fao_wheat) +
  geom_line(mapping=aes(
    x=Year,
    y=(Value - mean(Value))/sd(Value),
    group=Area,
    color=Area
  ))

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups
text:
Group-level Calculation in a Visualization


Code
ggplot(data=fao_wheat) +
  geom_line(mapping=aes(
    x=Year,
    y=(Value - mean(Value))/sd(Value),
    group=Area,
    color=Area
  )) +
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") +
  labs(
    title="Nordic Wheat Production",
    x="Year",
    y="Relative Production (z-score)",
    caption="Source: United Nations FAOSTAT",
    color="Country"

      "Finland" = "#002F6C", #Finland blue

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Agricultural Productivity
How should we measure agricultural productivity?


Productivity is a measure of how inputs are converted into outputs

What are inputs to agriculture?



Land
Labor
Water
Machinery (capital)
Fertilizer
etc

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Measuring Agricultural Productivity
How do we measure agricultural productivity?

One measure is Total Factor Productivity
Index measuring how efficiently agricultural inputs are transformed into agricultural outputs
Effectively a ratio of output to inputs
Easy when there is one input
More difficult when there are many

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
TFP in Practice
In practice we measure TFP as a function

Hold other inputs/factors constant
TFP is the “left over” productivity

What is the difficulty with this approach?


How do we make sure farmers hold inputs constant? (we can’t)
Other factors (e.g., weather) are impossible to hold constant
Do we care about productivity in the lab or on real farms?

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Estimating TFP
Estimating TFP is an empirical modeling problem

Collect data on all factors we think influence crop growth
Across many farms and many years
Use of inputs and other factors will vary across observations
Use this variation to isolate the impact of each factor on output
Combine this with actual input use to predict output for each observation
TFP is the “residual” (true value minus prediction)

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Challenges with Measuring TFP

Suppose we want to compute the change in TFP for many countries over time
We’ll use the method I outlined

Collect data on output, inputs, and other factors
Use it to construct an empirical model of productivity
TFP is the residual unexplained by the model

What challenges might we encounter?
What might you do to address those problems?

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Some Challenges Measuring TFP
Some challenges measuring TFP using observational data

Consistency in measurement both across time and space
Unmeasured factors (e.g., intensity of rain)
Unmeasured quality of inputs and output
Substitution between inputs
Crop switching
Many more!

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Is Measuring TFP Impossible?

There are many ways our estimates of TFP could go wrong
No set of estimates is “perfect”
Should we just give up?



TFP estimates provide valuable information, even if not “perfect”
Do the best job we can
Continue to improve (better data, models, etc)

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Measuring National Agricultural Production
Consistency of data is important for measuring TFP across countries and over time

Ideally measure output using methods that allow for comparing measurements

Across all countries
Across time

Include the majority of countries
Include a wide array of agricultural products

title: USDA NASS Data

About the USDA NASS
The US Department of Agriculture’s National Agricultural Statistics

Timely, accurate, and objective operational data
US domestic agricultural production.
Annual: Random sample survey of farms
Quinquennial: Full Census of Agriculture

Intended to be consistent and comparable for every US county

title: USDA NASS Data
text:
Goals of NASS

Report the facts on American agriculture
Objective and unbiased statistics on a preannounced schedule

Fair and impartial to all market participants

Safeguard the privacy of farmers, ranchers, and other data providers

title: USDA NASS Data
text:
Collected Data - Crops

Acreage: Acres planted, acres intended for planting, and acres harvested.
Yield & Production: Average yield per acre and total aggregate volume harvested

title: More Multivariate Modeling

Factor Parameter Estimates
You will always get one fewer factor parameter than the number of levels

If we include all factor parameters in the model
The intercept would be colinear with the factor parameters
Multiple combinations of values for the intercept and factor parameters give identical predictions
To solve this R:

Chooses one factor level and forces it to be zero (excludes it)
The intercept and remaining factor levels are now unique

R’s choice of level to exclude is arbitrary

Economically

You can only compare factor parameters against each other
Comparisons against zero are actually against the excluded level

title: More Multivariate Modeling
text:
Interplay between features
The typical linear model assumes the effect of each feature is independent
y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_n x_n + \epsilon

The effect of increasing x_1 is exactly b_1
Regardless of the value of other features

Are there circumstances where this might not hold?

title: More Multivariate Modeling
text:
Feature interactions
The effects of one feature may depend on the value of another feature

Drought is exacerbated by high temperatures
Low rain in the current month is moderated by rain in previous months
High temperatures are bad, but really high temperatures are worse

How could we think about accounting for these facts in our models?

title: More Multivariate Modeling
text:
Feature interactions
Mathematically you can include interactions offeatures

An additional term that is the product of two or more features

\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_{12} x_1 x_2

How much does \hat y change if x_1 increases by one? \frac{\partial \hat y}{\partial x_1} = b_1 + b_{12} x_2
The effect of x_1 depends on the size of x_2

title: More Multivariate Modeling
text:
Feature polynomials
You can interact a feature with itself
\hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_{11} x_1 x_1 - How much does \hat y change if x_1 increases by one? \frac{\partial \hat y}{\partial x_1} = 2 b_1 x_1 - Creates a nonlinear effect - The effect of a 1-unit increase in x_1 increases as x_1 increases

title: More Multivariate Modeling
text:
Interactions in R Models

Construct interaction features in R using the * operator
R includes both the interaction and the uninteracted features
e.g., y ~ x1 * x2 y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_{12} x_1 x_2

title: More Multivariate Modeling
text:
Polynomials in R Models

Construction polynomial interactions using the * operator
R includes both the interaction and uninteracted feature
e.g., y ~ x1 * x1 y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_{11} x_1 x_1

title: More Multivariate Modeling
text:
Higher-order interactions
You can construct higher order interactions

R includes all possible combinations of the individual features
y ~ x1*x2*x3 \begin{aligned}
y =& b_1 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + b_3 x_3 + \\
    & b_{12} x_1 x_2 + b_{13} x_1 x_3 + b_{23} x_2 x_3 + \\
    & b_{123} x_1 x_2 x_3
\end{aligned}

Modeling Basics
text:
Models - Framing Discussion
What is a model?

A simplified abstraction of reality

Purposefully designed to approximate some system or complex phenomenon
Intentionally simplified (why?)
Captures first-order behavior or relationships
Discards distracting noise or minutiae

title: Modeling Basics
section: What is the goal of a model?
text:
What is the goal of a model?
Real world systems are incredibly complex

Suppose a model ignores some biological and/or environmental realities

Is it still more useful than just looking at the raw historical data?
Why or why not?

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Evaluating models
What is a “good” model?

What properties will make us prefer one model over another?
How should we evaluate or compare potential models?
How should we make decisions over what features to include in a model?

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Many forms of models
Models come in many forms

Miniature analogs of physical objects (e.g., wind tunnel models)
Simplified biological systems in controlled environments
Sophisticated computer-based simulations
Mathematical representations of relationships in physical, biological, or economic systems

This class will focus on the mathematical representations

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Models as math
Models can be implemented as mathematical abstractions of the real world

Attempt to use information we know about the world

Called features, explanatory variables, or independent variables

To explain some outcome we care about

Called labels, response variables, or dependent variables

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Models as math
Some symbology

Labels are often denoted as y
The collection of features denoted as x

We are attempting to learn about the function
y = f(x) + \varepsilon
What is \varepsilon here?

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Breaking down models as math
Suppose we have the model: y = f(x) + \varepsilon

f(x) represents the relationship we want to uncover
\varepsilon represents the “noise”
Why is there “noise” in this process?
What contributes to noise?

title: Modeling Basics
section: What are the goals of modeling?
text:
What are the goals of modeling?
In general we will have one of two objectives in building models
Explanation

Determine causal and structural relationships
Focused on relationships between specific features and the label

Direction/Sign
Magnitude
Statistical Precision

Favors simple, interpretable models over predictive power
Focus on accounting for confounders

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Explanation Model Examples
Examples of questions that lead to explanation models:

Suppose average July temperatures increase by 1°C. How much do avocado yields change?
How much can we mitigate the impacts of drought on avocado yields using advanced fertilizers or technology?

title: Modeling Basics
section: What are the goals of modeling?
text:
What are the goals of modeling?
In general we will have one of two objectives in building models
Prediction

Use what we know about the world to make predictions of something we don’t know
Often using current conditions to predict the future
Focused on accurate and precise predictions of the label
Care about the quality of the prediction, not how individual features change predictions

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Prediction Model Examples
Examples of questions that lead to prediction models:

Given this year’s climate predictions, what do we expect avocado yields to be?
How do we expect avocado yields to change over the next 20 years?

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Evaluating Prediction Models
How do we decide if a prediction model is “good”?

Good predictions tend to have two attributes
Accuracy: Predictions are, on average, correct
Precision: Predictions have low noise or variability

Suppose I want to predict tomorrow’s high temperature

Model 1: I always predict it will be 75 degrees
Model 2: I always predict it will be today’s high temperature

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Ordinary Least Squares
We’ll use Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)

Assumes y is a linear function of

Features (x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n)
Unknown parameters (b_0, b_1, b_2, \dots, b_n)

Our prediction of the label \hat y is \hat y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_n x_n
OLS finds b values that minimize the Mean Square Error (MSE) of the predictions

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Mean Square Error
In OLS, we use MSE as the loss function

MSE is the average of squared prediction errors MSE = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( y_i - \hat y_i \right)^2
Perfect predictions have MSE of zero
MSE increases as predictions become less accurate
Models with lower MSE have “better” predictions

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Loss Functions
Building a model requires choosing a loss function

Allows comparing different types of prediction errors
In general, loss functions increase as model predictions get “worse”
Attempt to find models that minimize the loss function
The loss function embeds your preferences over different types of prediction errors

title: Modeling Basics
text:
Why OLS?
Why do we use OLS in this class?

Simple, linear relationship is a good starting point for modeling
Mathematical trick makes it “easy” to find b values that minimize MSE
Predictions from OLS have desirable properties

OLS is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE)
“Best” means most precise
“Unbiased” means predictions are correct on average

Other Models
There are many other modeling approaches used in the real world

Relax or fully abandon the linear functional form
Trade some bias for improved precision
Implement alternative loss functions
Address cases where there are many features to choose between

What are Cross Joins?
In the last class we discussed Cross Joins (many-to-many)

Joins form all possible matches of data between the two data frames
If an row in the left table matches multiple rows in the right table

R creates one copy of the left table row for each match

Same for rows in the right table matching multiple rows in the left table

Right: 3 rows with Year == 1990 & ISO3 == "USA"

title: Advanced Joins

title: Advanced Joins
section: Types of inequality joins: Pure Inequality
text:
Types of inequality joins: Pure Inequality
Inequality Conditions

Match when the value in the left table is <, <=, >, >= to the value in the right table
The join expression is e.g.,

<left_col> >= <right_col>

title: Advanced Joins
section: Types of inequality joins: Pure Inequality
text:
Types of inequality joins: Pure Inequality
Inequality Conditions

Will form every possible combination that satisfies this condition
e.g., join_by(ISO3,Year >= Year) will

Require exact matches of ISO3
Match all observations where left Year is greater than or equal to right year

Can lead to cross-join like explosions of observations

title: Advanced Joins
text:
Types of inequality joins: Rolling

Sometimes you’d like to find the closest unequal match
e.g., Dates don’t precisely match between left and right table

For each date in the left table
Find the observation in the right table with the closest date on or after the date in the left table

The closest() helper restricts a relationship to the single closest match
Place the relationship expression inside closest()
If no observation satisfies the inequality, there is no match

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Measuring Agricultural Productivity
How do we measure agricultural productivity?

One measure is Total Factor Productivity
Index measuring how efficiently agricultural inputs are transformed into agricultural outputs
Effectively a ratio of output to inputs
Easy when there is one input
More difficult when there are many

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
TFP in Practice
In practice we measure TFP as a function

Hold other inputs/factors constant
TFP is the “left over” productivity

What is the difficulty with this approach?


How do we make sure farmers hold inputs constant? (we can’t)
Other factors (e.g., weather) are impossible to hold constant
Do we care about productivity in the lab or on real farms?

title: FAOSTAT Data and Visualization
text:
Estimating TFP
Estimating TFP is an empirical modeling problem

Collect data on all factors we think influence crop growth
Across many farms and many years
Use of inputs and other factors will vary across observations
Use this variation to isolate the impact of each factor on output
Combine this with actual input use to predict output for each observation
TFP is the “residual” (true value minus prediction)

Collect data on output, inputs, and other factors
Use it to construct an empirical model of productivity
TFP is the residual unexplained by the model

What challenges might we encounter?

Some challenges measuring TFP using observational data

Consistency in measurement both across time and space
Unmeasured factors (e.g., intensity of rain)

Many more!

There are many ways our estimates of TFP could go wrong
No set of estimates is “perfect”
Should we just give up?



TFP estimates provide valuable information, even if not “perfect”
Do the best job we can
Continue to improve (better data, models, etc)

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
section: CSV has been a de facto standard for data
text:
CSV has been a de facto standard for data
The Bottleneck:

Modern datasets like high-resolution climate rasters or satellite indices overwhelm plain text formats like CSV

e.g., The FAO data is nearly 400 MB in CSV format

Data stored in purely text format

Requires software “guess” properties of the data
Numeric data needs to be translated from text
Repeated text values written out in full, each time

CSV files are

Slow to read
Large
Require guesses or manual intervention to read correctly

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Modern Big Data Storage
The Next Generation:
Define a data file format for modern big data

Portable: Works across data processing systems
Fast: Information you need loads quickly
Compact: Data stored efficiently for small files
Consistent: All software interprets the data identically without guessing

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
The Parquet Format
Parquet (PAR-kay) is a modern data file format for storing tidy data frames

Created in 2013
Specification is free and open source
Managed by the Apache Foundation
Implemented in most data analysis software

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Column-orientation
Column-oriented storage

In CSV files data are oriented in rows

You must read all of one row before moving on to the next
Inefficient if you only want data from specific columns

Parquet files use a column format

Only need to read data for the columns you request

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Automatic Compression
Automatic Compression

A CSV must write out every value in every cell as text
Parquet automatically compresses information

Column-oriented files are more compressible in general
Dictionary compression of frequent values
Run-length encoding for repeated values
Delta-encoding efficiently packs sequential numbers/timestamps

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Strict Schema
Strict Schema

A CSV file doesn’t contain any information about data types
Parquet files explicitly define data types of each column

Integer, Floating point, Character, Boolean, Date, and Timestamp data types

Parquet uses explicit formats for each data type (e.g., IEEE-754 floating point)
Any data processing package interprets each value the exact same way
Explicit support for missing (NA) values

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Disadvantages

Binary files aren’t human-readable
Column-oriented format makes “appending” data slow

Poorly suited for cases where you frequently update data

Performance gains only materialize on larger files

1000s of observations
10s or 100s of columns

text:

Parquet much smaller, so they load quickly

Choosing a Visualization File Format
You have several choices for file formats, which have advantages and disadvantages

PDF files best for publication quality graphics

Are vector images, they scale up flawlessly to very large image sizes
Complicated visualizations make large output file that load slowly

PNG files best for general use

Are raster images, they will get blocky as you scale them up
Files will be a fixed size no matter how complicated the visualization

JPG files best for websites/text messages

Also raster images but use Lossy Compression
Files tend to be very small, nearly anyone can view them
Underlying compression algorithm can lose details

There are other, more niche formats available too

Viridis Palettes
Viridis palates are designed

To be clear even if the viewer has common forms of colorblindness

To have strongly contrasting colors with a logical order of progression

title: Data Visualization with Multiple Groups

Viridis Scales
The correct Viridis scale to use depends on your data:

scale_color_viridis_b()

Binned: Discrete with a defined order/ranking
Adjacent values have similar colors

scale_color_viridis_c()

Continuous: A range where any value is possible

scale_color_viridis_d()

Discrete: Discrete but unordered
Maximizes contrast between colors

Combining Data from Multiple Data Frames
Think about two data frames that may contain similar information

Separate files for different measurements (e.g., CRU)
Separate files for different time periods
Separate files for different places

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Tidyverse methods for combining data
The tidyverse has several methods of combining data frames

bind_rows() stacks rows of data frames
bind_cols() stacks columns of data frames
Joins use more complicated logic to match rows between datasets

Covered next week

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Stacking Rows
bind_rows() stacks rows of multiple data frames

Each data frame is added to the bottom of the previous data frame
Useful when you have multiple data frames with the same layout

Identical column names
Identical data types

e.g.,

One data frame for each year of data
Otherwise identical

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Stacking Rows
bind_rows()

Returns a single data frame, aligning columns by name
Fills in with NA when a column doesn’t exist







Watch out for inconsistent data types!


Each column needs a single data type. R will attempt to coerce values of each column to a single data type, but won’t convert numbers to text or vice versa. This can lead to unexpected NA values if you try to stack a column that switches between text and numeric data!

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Two ways to use bind_rows()


Just stack data frames
bind_rows(data_2000,data_2001)




Stack rows from each data fame
But otherwise no way to tell them apart



Stack with identifier column
bind_rows(
  list(
    "2000" = data_2000, 
    "2001" = data_2001
  ),
  .id="Year"
)
Adds a Year column with the corresponding name from the list()

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Stacking Columns
bind_cols() stacks columns of multiple data frames

Each data frame is added to the right of the previous data frame
Useful when you have multiple data frames of information for the same observations

Observations align perfectly across each data frame
Column names do not overlap

e.g., a wide table was split up into multiple files

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Stacking Columns
In general you won’t use bind_rows()

Few cases where you need to combine columns across data frames by matching rows
Only useful when you have full knowledge of the provenance of each data frame, e.g.,

You intentionally split off columns from a data frame
Want to combine back later

No checks for whether observations are correctly aligned
Usually use Joins to match observations across dataframes (next week)

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Reshaping Data Overview
What does it mean to reshape (pivot) data?


Take information organized by columns and reorganize in rows or vice-versa
Will change the shape of your data frame

pivot_longer()

New data are longer and narrower
More rows, fewer columns
Column information translated into rows

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Reshaping Data Overview
What does it mean to reshape (pivot) data?
pivot_wider()

New data are wider and narrower
More columns, fewer rows
Row information is translated into columns

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Reshaping Data - The Old Way

The pivot functions are relatively new
The tidyverse previously used gather and spread
They have the superseded lifecycle tag
No new features will be added, but won’t be removed soon
Harder to use, Fewer features
Avoid using them

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Using pivot_wider()
When you use pivot_wider() you should ask yourself three questions:

Which column(s) will uniquely identify observation in my new data frame? id_cols
Which column(s) contain information that will be used to construct new column names? names_from
Which column(s) contain values that will populate those new columns? values_from

Each answer tells you what to use for each of the required arguments!

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Example pivot_wider()
I would like to create a new version of the CRU data frame

One row for each Country-Year
Columns for the temperature in each month

How can I do this?

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Example pivot_wider()

One row for each Country-Year
Columns for the temperature in each month


Which column(s) will uniquely identify observation in my new data frame? id_cols
Which column(s) contain information that will be used to construct new column names? names_from
Which column(s) contain values that will populate those new columns? values_from

title: More Data Wrangling
text:
Example pivot_wider()

id_cols = c(Year,Country)
names_from = Period
values_from = Value







Remove extra columns before pivoting


When pivot_wider() rearranges your data frame it needs to know what to do with information in each column. This is ambiguous for any column that doesn’t show up in one of the three arguments. You should remove columns that aren’t needed with select() before pivoting.

title: Relational Data

Joining Data Frames in R
Perform joins in R using
join_*(<left_df>,<right_df>,by=<relationships>)

<left_df> - The “left” data frame
<right_df> - The “right” data frame
<relationships> - Vector of relationships

Columns that define how to match observations
Column names must be in quotes
Form a match whenever relationships have identical values

title: Relational Data
text:
Types of Joins
R has the following primary types of joins

inner_join keep only observations that match in both data frames
left_join keep all observations from the left data frame and matches from the right
right_join keep all observations from the right data frame and matches from the left
full_join keep all observations from both left and right data frame

title: Relational Data
text:
Types of Joins
R has the following additional joins

semi_join keep all observations from the left data frame that have a match in the right

Does not duplicate observations from the left data frame
Does not include columns from the right data frame

anti_join keep all observations from the left data frame that do not have a match in the right

Does not duplicate observations from the left data frame
Does not include columns from the right data frame
Useful for tracking down join errors

.x to the column name from the left table

What is this information?

term: Name of the feature associated with this parameter (x_i)
estimate: Model’s estimated value of the parameter (b_i)
std_error: A measure of the statistical uncertainty in the parameter estimate
statistic: The t-statistic of a hypothesis test the true parameter is equal to zero
p_value: The p-value of this hypothesis test
lower_ci: The lower bound of the 95% Confidence Interval of the estimated parameter
upper_ci: The upper bound of the 95% Confidence Interval of the estimated parameter

title: More Modeling

Much of the information in this table relates to statistical properties of the estimated parameters

This is not a course in econometrics or statistics

Need to be adjusted for peculiarities of your data

title: More Modeling

Adding more data or running the analysis on new data unlikely to substantially alter the estimate of the parameter
Small standard errors increase your confidence you have a reliable estimate

title: More Modeling

lower_ci and upper_ci are bounds on the 95% confidence interval of the estimated parameter
A measure of the range of parameter values you might have seen
The model’s best guess of

If you collected new data and repeated this process many times
95% of the parameter estimates would fall in this range

Narrow confidence intervals increase your confidence you have a reliable estimate
Suggest estimates outside that range are unlikely

Why Multivariate Models

Multivariate Models
Multivariate models include multiple features y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + b_n x_n + \epsilon

Simultaneously account for each feature (x_1 to x_n)
Each parameter (b_1 to b_n) represents

Effect of the associated feature on the label
Holding all other features constant

Numerically evaluating models
Graphical evaluations of models are useful but limited

Quickly give a sense of accuracy, precision, and potential pitfalls
Comparisons won’t always be definitive

title: Multivariate Modeling
text:
Measures of model fit/performance

OLS uses MSE as its loss function

A single number that evaluates prediction errors on the training data
Zero means a “perfect” model
Larger numbers mean predictions are less “good”

OLS chooses the model parameters that mathematically minimize the loss function

No other choice of parameters can reduce the MSE

We would tend to prefer models with lower MSE
MSE is not the only metric for model performance

title: Multivariate Modeling
text:
Model performance metrics
The computed metrics are

r_squared - The R-Squared Statistic

Squared correlation between model predictions and actual values
Ranges from 0 to 1
Values close to 1 mean predictions more strongly correlated with actual values

In OLS adding features will always reduce the R-squared!

Regardless of whether the feature is “relevant”

title: Multivariate Modeling
text:
Model performance metrics
The computed metrics are

adj_r_squared - The Adjusted R-Squared

The R-squared, reduced by a factor related to the number of model features
Typically ranges from 0 to 1, but can be negative
Values close to 1 mean predictions strongly correlated with actual values

In OLS adding features may increase or decrease the Adjusted R-Squared

The penalty scales with features/observations

title: Multivariate Modeling
text:
Model performance metrics
The computed metrics are

mse - The Mean Squared Error

The loss function in OLS
Values close to zero mean predictions are close to actual values

In OLS adding features will always reduce the MSE

Regardless of whether the feature is “relevant”

rmse is the square root of MSE

title: Multivariate Modeling
text:
Model performance metrics
The other metrics

sigma - Variance of the model residual
statistic - The statistic from an F-test that all parameters (excluding the intercept) are zero
p-value - The p-value of the above F-test
df - The Model Degrees of Freedom from the above F-test
nobs - The number of observations in the training data

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
section: CSV has been a de facto standard for data
text:
CSV has been a de facto standard for data
The Bottleneck:

Modern datasets like high-resolution climate rasters or satellite indices overwhelm plain text formats like CSV

e.g., The FAO data is nearly 400 MB in CSV format

Data stored in purely text format

Requires software “guess” properties of the data
Numeric data needs to be translated from text
Repeated text values written out in full, each time

CSV files are

Slow to read
Large
Require guesses or manual intervention to read correctly

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Modern Big Data Storage
The Next Generation:
Define a data file format for modern big data

Portable: Works across data processing systems
Fast: Information you need loads quickly
Compact: Data stored efficiently for small files
Consistent: All software interprets the data identically without guessing

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
The Parquet Format
Parquet (PAR-kay) is a modern data file format for storing tidy data frames

Created in 2013
Specification is free and open source
Managed by the Apache Foundation
Implemented in most data analysis software

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Column-orientation
Column-oriented storage

In CSV files data are oriented in rows

You must read all of one row before moving on to the next
Inefficient if you only want data from specific columns

Parquet files use a column format

Only need to read data for the columns you request

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Automatic Compression
Automatic Compression

A CSV must write out every value in every cell as text
Parquet automatically compresses information

Column-oriented files are more compressible in general
Dictionary compression of frequent values
Run-length encoding for repeated values
Delta-encoding efficiently packs sequential numbers/timestamps

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Advantages: Strict Schema
Strict Schema

A CSV file doesn’t contain any information about data types
Parquet files explicitly define data types of each column

Integer, Floating point, Character, Boolean, Date, and Timestamp data types

Parquet uses explicit formats for each data type (e.g., IEEE-754 floating point)
Any data processing package interprets each value the exact same way
Explicit support for missing (NA) values

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet Disadvantages

Binary files aren’t human-readable
Column-oriented format makes “appending” data slow

Poorly suited for cases where you frequently update data

Performance gains only materialize on larger files

1000s of observations
10s or 100s of columns

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Parquet in this Class
In this class I will provide Parquet versions of most data files

Data files contain many, repeated text values
Very large CSV files
Parquet much smaller, so they load quickly
Strict schema, so everyone gets the same data
ELMS and gmail understand they are data files

text:
Saving Visualizations
Visualizations are most useful if you can share them

R Studio’s Plots viewer allows saving visualizations

Several steps
Not Automated
Required every time you update the visualization

You can add code to save a visualization with ggsave()

Visualization will be saved each time you run your R code
Apply specific options to the saved file (file format, size)

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Using ggsave
To save a visualization use
ggsave(<output_path>)

R determines the output format using the file extension

e.g., .png, .jpg, .pdf

Some important optional arguments are:

plot: A variable containing the plot to save

Otherwise, the default is the last plot generated

width: Width of the saved image in inches
height: Height of the saved image in inches

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Example Saving a Visualization

# Set a path to a directory where you can save files
homedir_path = "/home/username/Documents/AREC280"

ggsave(
  file.path(homedir_path,"wine_production.png"),
  plot=production_viz,
  width=16,
  height=9
)







No write permissions to the Data folder


You do not have permission to write files to the Data folder in the class Google drive. Attempting to save a file to that folder will result in a Permission Denied error.
Be sure to save to a folder on your local computer.

title: Data Visualization and Parquet Files
text:
Choosing a Visualization File Format
You have several choices for file formats, which have advantages and disadvantages

PDF files best for publication quality graphics

Are vector images, they scale up flawlessly to very large image sizes
Complicated visualizations make large output file that load slowly

PNG files best for general use

Are raster images, they will get blocky as you scale them up
Files will be a fixed size no matter how complicated the visualization

JPG files best for websites/text messages

Also raster images but use Lossy Compression
Files tend to be very small, nearly anyone can view them
Underlying compression algorithm can lose details

There are other, more niche formats available too
